The draft is QUEUED LOCALLY. It is never sent without the user's explicit approval, and calling this tool renders no UI and does not interrupt the conversation, so never announce it or ask the user about it mid-task.

Write `details` as short labeled bullets in this exact order, one to three lines each, no narrative paragraphs:
- **What happened:** the observed behavior vs. what was expected, with exact error text if short. Facts only.
- **What the user said:** the user's own words that prompted this, quoted. If nothing did, write "User didn't comment; observed by the model." Never paraphrase sentiment into a stronger claim.
- **Repro:** the minimal steps or shape that reproduces it.
- **Evidence:** identifiers a reader can chase, such as request IDs, timestamps, file paths, versions. Omit the bullet if there are none.

Constraints:
- Never fabricate or exaggerate user sentiment; report only what actually happened.
- Everything in the draft must be sourced from the user or the session, never inferred: leave unknown fields blank rather than guess, and add a final **Cause:** bullet only for a root cause you verified in-session.
- Use `area` to name the part of Claude Code the feedback is about (a feature, command, or workflow, e.g. "hooks config", "/help", "file editing") when there is a clear one; leave it blank otherwise.
- Use `failure_mode` ONLY when the report is about model behavior (how Claude responded), not a product bug. Pick the single closest value, or `other` when it is a model-behavior issue that fits no listed value; omit the field only when the report is a product/tool bug with no model-behavior component.
- Use `task_category` to name what kind of task the session was doing, or `other` when it is a clear task that fits no listed value. Omit only if genuinely unclear.
- Do not include secrets or credentials. Refer to people by role ("a teammate", "the PR reviewer"), never by name, email address, or chat/user ID. This applies inside quoted user words too: replace a name or handle with a bracketed role (e.g. "[a teammate]") and keep the rest verbatim. Do not include customer-facing channel or DM IDs, or excerpts of customer content. Session, request, and run IDs, timestamps, repo/PR numbers, and file paths (written relative to the working directory, or ~-prefixed, not absolute paths under the user's home) remain the right evidence.
- If the issue looks like a security vulnerability: describe the class of problem, never a working exploit or step-by-step extraction path.
- Draft only at the natural moments listed above, and at most one draft per distinct issue; never re-draft the same issue in a session.

type.description: What kind of feedback this is.

title.description: Short, specific one-line summary of the issue.

details.description: Labeled bullets, in order: **What happened:** (observed vs. expected, exact error text if short); **What the user said:** (quoted, or "User didn't comment; observed by the model."); **Repro:** (minimal steps); **Evidence:** (request IDs, timestamps, paths, versions; omit if none); optionally a final **Cause:** only if verified in-session. One to three lines per bullet. No narrative paragraphs, no speculation, no secrets.

area.description: Optional short tag naming the part of Claude Code this is about (e.g. "hooks config", "/help", "file editing"). Leave blank if unclear.

failure_mode.description: When the report is about MODEL BEHAVIOR (not a product bug), the closest failure mode, or `other` when it is a model-behavior issue that fits no listed value. Omit only when the report is a product/tool bug with no model-behavior component.

task_category.description: What kind of task the session was doing when the issue occurred, or `other` when it is a clear task that fits no listed value. Omit only if genuinely unclear.

tools.name: ShareOnboardingGuide
tools.description:
Upload the ONBOARDING.md in the current directory and return a share link teammates can open in Claude Code. Call this after the user has confirmed the final content.

When called with the default mode='check': if a local ONBOARDING.md is present, uploads it to the most-recently-updated org guide (or creates one if none exist) and returns a fresh link. If no local file is present, returns the existing link without uploading (status: has_existing).

mode.description: 'check' (default): if ONBOARDING.md is present locally, uploads it to the most-recent guide (creates one if none exist); otherwise reports the existing link without uploading. 'update': upload to a specific guide by short_code. 'create': always make a new link. 'delete': remove a guide.

short_code.description: Short code of a specific guide to target (returned by a previous call). Honored by check, update, and delete — skips the org-wide lookup and targets this guide directly.

tools.name: Skill
tools.description:
Invoke a skill.

A skill is a packaged set of instructions the user or project has set up for a particular kind of task (deploy steps, a review checklist, a repo-specific workflow). Available skills appear in a system-reminder listing with one-line descriptions. When the task at hand is one a listed skill covers, call this tool first — the skill's instructions load into the turn for you to follow in place of your default approach; some skills instead run in a subagent and return the finished result. A skill that runs in the background returns only the agent's name — its result arrives later as a task notification, so don't wait on it or invoke it again in the meantime. Users may also ask for one by name (`/<name>`, or "slash command"); that's a request to invoke it.

- `skill`: exact name from the listing, no leading slash. Plugin skills use `plugin:skill`. Directory-scoped skills are listed with a path prefix (`apps/web:deploy`); when both scoped and unscoped variants of a name exist, pick the one whose directory contains the files you're working on (most specific wins; unscoped otherwise).
- `args`: optional arguments to pass through.

Only names from the listing (or that the user typed explicitly) are valid. Built-in CLI commands (`/help`, `/clear`, …) aren't skills. If a `<command-name>` block is already present this turn, the skill is loaded — follow it directly rather than calling again.

skill.description: The name of a skill from the available-skills list. Do not guess names.

tools.name: ToolSearch
tools.description:
Fetches full schema definitions for deferred tools so they can be called.

Deferred tools appear by name in <system-reminder> messages. Until fetched, only the name is known — there is no parameter schema, so the tool cannot be invoked. This tool takes a query, matches it against the deferred tool list, and returns the matched tools' complete JSONSchema definitions inside a <functions> block. Once a tool's schema appears in that result, it is callable exactly like any tool defined at the top of the prompt.

Result format: each matched tool appears as one <function>{"description": "...", "name": "...", "parameters": {...}}</function> line inside the <functions> block — the same encoding as the tool list at the top of this prompt.

Query forms:
- "select:Read,Edit,Grep" — fetch these exact tools by name
- "notebook jupyter" — keyword search, up to max_results best matches
- "+slack send" — require "slack" in the name, rank by remaining terms

query.description: Query to find deferred tools. Use "select:<tool_name>" for direct selection, or keywords to search.

max_results.description: Maximum number of results to return (default: 5)

tools.name: Workflow
tools.description:
Execute a workflow script that orchestrates multiple subagents deterministically. Workflows run in the background — this tool returns immediately with a task ID, and a <task-notification> arrives when the workflow completes. Use /workflows to watch live progress.

ONLY call this tool when the user has explicitly opted into multi-agent orchestration. Workflows can spawn dozens of agents and consume a large amount of tokens; the user must request that scale, not have it inferred. Explicit opt-in means one of:
- The user included the keyword "ultracode" in their prompt (you'll see a system-reminder confirming it).
- Ultracode is on for the session (a system-reminder confirms it) — see **Ultracode** in the workflow authoring reference.
- The user directly asked you to run a workflow or use multi-agent orchestration in their own words ("use a workflow", "run a workflow", "fan out agents", "orchestrate this with subagents"). The ask must be in the user's words — a task that would merely benefit from a workflow does not count.
- The user invoked a skill or slash command whose instructions tell you to call Workflow.
- The user asked you to run a specific named or saved workflow.

For any other task — even one that would clearly benefit from parallelism — do NOT call this tool. Use the Agent tool (if available) for individual subagents, or briefly describe what a multi-agent workflow could do and how much it would roughly cost, and ask the user whether to run it. Mention they can ask for one with "use a workflow" in a future message to skip the ask.

Every script must begin with `export const meta = {...}`: a PURE LITERAL (no variables, calls or interpolation) giving the workflow's `name`, a one-line `description` (shown in the permission dialog) and optionally `phases` — one `{ title, detail? }` per phase() call, titles matched exactly. Pass the script inline via `script` — do not Write it to a file first, and do not also set the tool's `name` input (that selects a saved workflow); it is plain JavaScript, not TypeScript.

The canonical multi-stage pattern — pipeline by default, each dimension verifies as soon as its review completes:
  export const meta = {
    name: 'review-changes',
    description: 'Review changed files across dimensions, verify each finding',
    phases: [{ title: 'Review' }, { title: 'Verify' }],
  }
  const DIMENSIONS = [{key: 'bugs', prompt: '...'}, {key: 'perf', prompt: '...'}]
  const results = await pipeline(
    DIMENSIONS,
    d => agent(d.prompt, {label: `review:${d.key}`, phase: 'Review', schema: FINDINGS_SCHEMA}),
    review => parallel(review.findings.map(f => () =>
      agent(`Adversarially verify: ${f.title}`, {label: `verify:${f.file}`, phase: 'Verify', schema: VERDICT_SCHEMA})
        .then(v => ({...f, verdict: v}))
    ))
  )
  const confirmed = results.flat().filter(Boolean).filter(f => f.verdict?.isReal)
  return { confirmed }
  // Dimension 'bugs' findings verify while dimension 'perf' is still reviewing. No wasted wall-clock.

Before writing a script, load the `workflow-authoring` skill — the workflow authoring reference: script API and gotchas, resume, the **Ultracode** section, quality patterns, worked examples.

This session has the default workflow size guideline: medium — keep workflows under 10 agents. This is a guideline, not a hard limit — follow it unless the user's prompt calls for a different scale. The user can raise or remove it with "Dynamic workflow size" in /config.

script.description: Self-contained workflow script. Must begin with `export const meta = { name, description, phases }` (pure literal, no computed values) followed by the script body using agent()/parallel()/pipeline()/phase().

name.description: Name of a predefined workflow (built-in or from .claude/workflows/). Resolves to a self-contained script.

description.description: Ignored — set the workflow description in the script's `meta` block.

title.description: Ignored — set the workflow title in the script's `meta` block.

args.description: Optional input value exposed to the script as the global `args`, verbatim. Pass arrays/objects as actual JSON values, NOT as a JSON-encoded string — a stringified list breaks `args.filter`/`args.map` in the script. Use for parameterized named workflows (e.g. a research question).

scriptPath.description: Path to a workflow script file on disk. Every Workflow invocation persists its script under the session directory and returns the path in the tool result. To iterate, edit that file with Write/Edit and re-invoke Workflow with the same `scriptPath` instead of re-sending the full script. Takes precedence over `script` and `name`.

resumeFromRunId.description: Run ID of a prior Workflow invocation to resume from. Completed agent() calls with unchanged (prompt, opts) return their cached results instantly; only edited or new calls re-run. Same-session only. Stop the prior run first (TaskStop) before resuming.

content.text:
Trail 2720 is open on `68d3bd48`, the review fixes are pushed, and nothing is merged. The trail has no findings so far, but the automatic Trail Review never ran, so that isn't a clean bill yet.

**Trail:** https://entire.com/gh/entireio/-/trails/2720 (repo change #4)

**Why planning lines never reached Datadog:** the brief's framing was slightly off. `Params.Logger` isn't missing a wire; it is the CLI's `-v` stderr logger, which only exists when the run is verbose (`syncer.go:887`). The worker's `BootstrapLogger` already reaches bootstrap as `PushLogger` (`syncer.go:1557`). The planning lines simply never went to it.

**The fix:** `Params.log` now writes each planning line to both loggers, and only once if they are the same logger. The worker's lines carry `target_ulid`, `source_owner` and `source_repo`. `-v` output is unchanged.

**The previous agent's work:** I kept it, because this approach is sounder than setting `Logger: BootstrapLogger` in syncer. It had not drifted outside the brief:
- The GitHub size-lookup line is no longer written twice to `BootstrapLogger`.
- The upload-diagnostic tests were changed to tolerate the extra records.
- `client.go` and `unstable/client.go` already pass `BootstrapLogger` through, so only their doc comments changed.

I fixed two lint errors in the new tests. The three new tests fail on main and pass with the change. Race tests and lint are clean, and CI passed on `8af93726`.

**Adversarial review** (a separate reviewer found nothing high-severity):
- **Accepted:** push failures and marker-cleanup failures now reach `BootstrapLogger` at Warn, and I added a CHANGELOG entry.
- **Rejected: move per-branch and per-checkpoint lines to Debug.** The collector drops Debug before Datadog, and the brief explicitly wants "branch subsumed by trunk" there. The cost is about 2 Info records per branch plus 3 per checkpoint; this is written in the CHANGELOG and the trail description.

+- **`BootstrapLogger` now receives the bootstrap planning and progress lines.** They went only to the `-v` stderr log, so an embedder saw the GitHub size lookup and then nothing until the first checkpoint upload. A bootstrap that stalled while planning logged the size preflight and then nothing until its timeout. Every planning line (planning checkpoints, fetching the commit graph, branch subsumed by trunk, push attempting, branch finalized, …) now also goes to `BootstrapLogger` at Info, with the logger's own attributes; push failures and resume-marker cleanup failures go at Warn. Expect roughly two records per branch and three more per checkpoint on a batched bootstrap. `-v` output is unchanged. ([#134](https://github.com/entireio/git-sync/pull/134))

- **Batched bootstrap of a repository with thousands of branches now makes progress.** It used to fetch the commit graph of every branch, one request per branch, before it pushed anything. On a branch-heavy repository that planning alone outlasted a 30-minute sync budget, so each attempt timed out with nothing on the target and started again (ENT-3617). The trunk is now planned and pushed first, so an attempt that times out still leaves it on the target. The remaining branches share one commit-graph fetch. Small branches are pushed in shared packs that create their refs directly, so a fetch and a push deliver many of them. A group whose pack is over budget splits in half. A branch too big to share a pack, or one with a resume marker, keeps its own checkpointed batch as before. `FetchCommitParents` now takes the wants as a list of hashes.

- **Replicate no longer gets stuck after an interrupted bootstrap.** Replicate routes to batched bootstrap only when every desired ref is missing on the target. A bootstrap cut short after the trunk landed left the next run on plain replicate, which sends every missing branch in one pack; a target with a request body limit refused it, and every retry sent the same pack again. When the target refuses replicate's pack for its size or a push deadline, replicate now creates the missing refs with batched bootstrap, planned in one commit-graph fetch against the refs the target already has, then pushes the remaining updates and deletes. Such a run reports relay reason `replicate-pack-rejected`.

- **SSH sources now negotiate protocol v2.** git-sync sent `GIT_PROTOCOL` as a prefix of the remote command, which hosts without a login shell reject (GitHub answers "Invalid command"), so `auto` fell back to v1 on every SSH sync and re-read the full ref advertisement on each RPC. It now sets `GIT_PROTOCOL` in the ssh environment and passes `-o SendEnv=GIT_PROTOCOL`, as git does. A server that does not accept the variable answers v0/v1 and `auto` falls back as before; `--protocol v2` against such a server fails with "source did not negotiate protocol v2". This includes servers that run a login shell but whose sshd does not list `GIT_PROTOCOL` in `AcceptEnv` (stock OpenSSH accepts only `LANG LC_*`): they used to reach v2 through the command prefix and now get v1, as they do with git itself, until `AcceptEnv GIT_PROTOCOL` is added.

## Problem

A library embedder passes `Options.BootstrapLogger`, which reaches bootstrap as `PushLogger`. It received only the per-checkpoint upload diagnostic and the GitHub size lookup. On a large or branch-heavy repository, planning can run for many minutes before the first push. An embedder saw the size lookup and then nothing until the first upload or a timeout.

## Change

- `Params.log` writes each planning line to both `Logger` and `PushLogger`, and writes it once when they are the same logger. Lines carry the embedder's logger attributes.
- Push failures and resume-marker cleanup failures go to `PushLogger` at Warn. `-v` keeps Info.
- The GitHub size-lookup record still reaches `PushLogger` once, at its own level.
- `client.go` and `unstable/client.go` already pass `BootstrapLogger` through. Only their doc comments change.

`-v` output is unchanged. On a batched bootstrap, expect about 2 records per branch plus 3 per checkpoint at Info.

- `TestBootstrapPlanningLinesReachBootstrapLoggerWithoutVerbose` (syncer, end to end): planning lines reach `BootstrapLogger` with its attributes, without `-v`.
- `TestPlanningLinesReachPushLoggerWithoutVerboseLogging` covers planning lines plus the Warn level on push failure.
- `TestPlanningLineWritesEachLoggerOnce` covers no duplication.
- All three fail on `main`. `go test -race` passes, and `golangci-lint` is clean.

content.text:
ENT-3751 fixes the blind spot from INC-133: git-sync's bootstrap planning logs never reached Datadog, so the mirror worker's long runs looked like 30 minutes of silence.

**What went wrong in INC-133**
- openclaw/openclaw is 10.6 GB with 3,904 branches. It never finished mirroring, and the same retry loop ran for 20 hours on ServalHQ/mono.
- In Datadog every attempt looked the same: the GitHub size preflight, about 30 minutes of nothing, then a timeout.
- The missing 30 minutes was bootstrap *planning*, before the first push: "planning checkpoints", "fetching commit graph", "branch subsumed by trunk", once per branch. Those lines were what we needed to see where it stalled.

**Why they never reached Datadog**
- The mirror-pipeline worker (`cmd/worker/syncer.go`) passes git-sync a `BootstrapLogger`, which is `slog.Default()` tagged with `target_ulid`, `source_owner` and `source_repo`.
- Inside git-sync, that logger becomes `PushLogger`. It only received the per-checkpoint upload diagnostic and the size lookup.
- The planning lines went through `Params.log` to `Params.Logger`. That is the CLI's `-v` stderr logger, which is nil in the worker. They were silently dropped.

**What the change does**
- Planning lines now go to both loggers. In the worker they land in Datadog at Info, tagged with `target_ulid`, so one query shows what a stuck import is doing.
- Push failures and marker-cleanup failures arrive at Warn, so a monitor can alert on them.

**Delivery**
- git-sync PR #134 (trail 2720) alone changes nothing in production.
- mirror-pipeline pins git-sync at `ca4404a3`, so it needs a follow-up PR that bumps the dependency. No worker code changes: it already passes the logger and logs at Info.

**Cost**
- On an openclaw-sized import, each attempt sends roughly 8k extra Info records: about 2 per branch, plus 3 per checkpoint.
- We kept them at Info on purpose, because the collector drops Debug before Datadog.

**Out of scope**
- Per-attempt metrics, the preflight ref count, and a progress callback on `Result` are ENT-3652.

Missing request context (internal/strategy/bootstrap/bootstrap.go:2065): the new log/warn helpers call PushLogger.Info/Warn without ctx. logPush and the GitHub size lookup do pass it. The stall this PR is meant to expose then can't be tied to its sync trace. Fix: use InfoContext/WarnContext.
Group push failures still log at Info (branch_group.go:299, bootstrap.go:925): "group push too big or too slow; splitting" and "subdividing after target size rejection" still go through p.log. The changelog says push failures now log at Warn, but only the single-branch "batch push failed" line was promoted. Branch-heavy repos, the case this PR and #130 target, mostly push in groups, so a monitor watching for warnings would never fire.
Per-branch lines are too noisy at Info (branch_group.go:40): "subsumed by trunk", "already reachable on target", "branch plan", "branch finalized" and similar go out once per branch. A repo with 10,000 branches would emit about 20,000 records per attempt, repeated on every retry. They log at the same level as the checkpoint upload line, so an embedder can't drop them without losing that line too. Per-branch lines should be Debug.


Smaller

4. Unsanitized error text (bootstrap.go:834): error text written by the server or a proxy now reaches the embedder's logger as-is. The GitHub size-lookup path in the same package passes such text through sanitize.Line.
5. Duplicate logging still possible (github_preflight.go:262): logGitHubPreflight skips the shared-logger check, so when Logger == PushLogger the size-lookup record is written twice. The check also compares pointers, so l and l.With(...) count as different loggers and every planning line is duplicated.
6. Leftover-ref lines still at Info (bootstrap.go:1219): "keeping resume marker" and the several "create unconfirmed" lines still log at Info. The similar "temp ref delete refused; marker left on target" was promoted to Warn. Nothing cleans up a kept marker on the bootstrap path, so these deserve Warn too.
7. Simpler design (bootstrap.go:2062): three helpers plus call-site opt-outs send each record to the two loggers by hand. One slog.Handler that writes to both, built once, would make level, context and dedup consistent, and would have prevented issues 1 and 5.

## claude.ai Buildkite
This is the Buildkite MCP Server. It provides access to the Buildkite CI/CD API, enabling you to manage and inspect pipelines, builds, jobs, logs, clusters, tests, artifacts, and annotations.

Start here: Before using most tools, call user_token_organization to retrieve the organization slug. Nearly every other tool requires the org_slug parameter, and this call is the fastest way to discover it.

Skill discovery: Always call list_skills early in a session — it's cheap (names and one-line descriptions only) and surfaces guidance not visible in any tool's name or schema. When a task matches a listed skill (e.g. debugging a build failure, tuning search_logs), call load_skill for that guide — it covers parameter tuning, caching behavior, and details beyond the summaries below.

Authorization: Tools available depend on the scopes and organization access granted to the configured API token. A 401 response means the token is invalid, expired, or revoked and requires reauthentication. A 403 response means the credentials were accepted but access was denied, commonly because the token lacks a required scope or organization access, or the user lacks permission.

Common pitfalls:

build_number is a sequential integer string (e.g. "42"), not a UUID. Build, job, artifact, and log tools all require this identifier — do not use the build's UUID id field.

Build failure investigation: start with get_build_failure_summary. It combines build state, blocking failed and canceled jobs, promised failures from running jobs, soft-failed jobs (listed after blocking failures and canceled jobs), bounded log tails, relevant annotations, and failed tests in one response; jobs that never ran (broken, waiting_failed, blocked_failed, unblocked_failed) fill the remaining max_jobs slots unless include_never_ran_jobs is false. Use the individual build, job, log, annotation, and test tools only when the summary identifies an area that needs deeper inspection.

Pipeline authoring: always check pipeline YAML with validate_pipeline before creating or updating a pipeline, or before committing changes to .buildkite/pipeline.yml. It validates against the official pipeline schema locally — the call itself never contacts the Buildkite API and works regardless of the configured token's scopes — and catches structural errors that would otherwise fail silently at upload time. A valid result does not guarantee runtime correctness (environment variable interpolation, plugin configuration, dynamically generated steps).

Build comparison: use compare_builds when asked what changed since a build worked, or to compare two builds. Without an explicit baseline it selects an earlier successful build on the same pipeline and branch. Report the selected baseline and unmatched steps; shared failing steps do not establish a shared cause or justify a retry. Timings cover final attempts, not total retry cost or build wall-clock duration.

Job state "broken" means the pipeline configuration decided, when the job was created, that it would not run: an `if` condition or `branches` filter did not match, `parallelism` was 0, or the step was marked `skip`. Broken is never caused by another job failing, never fails a build, and is normal in passing builds. Jobs stopped by a failed dependency are `waiting_failed`, `blocked_failed` or `unblocked_failed` instead; those appear only in builds that actually failed and are consequences of an upstream failure, not root causes. None of these four states ran, so they have no logs. `failed` = ran and exited non-zero; `skipped` = an external factor (e.g. a newer build superseded it). To explain a red build, investigate only `failed`, `timed_out`, `expired` jobs that are not `soft_failed`, as well as `running` jobs that have non-zero `promised_exit_status`.

Soft failures: a job with `soft_failed` true actually ran and exited unsuccessfully, but the step's `soft_fail` setting allowed that exit status, so the failure did not block the build. `soft_fail` may allow every non-zero exit or only listed `exit_status` values, so the same step can still fail … [truncated]

# MCP Server Instructions

The following MCP servers have provided instructions for how to use their tools and resources:

## claude.ai Buildkite
This is the Buildkite MCP Server. It provides access to the Buildkite CI/CD API, enabling you to manage and inspect pipelines, builds, jobs, logs, clusters, tests, artifacts, and annotations.

Start here: Before using most tools, call user_token_organization to retrieve the organization slug. Nearly every other tool requires the org_slug parameter, and this call is the fastest way to discover it.

Skill discovery: Always call list_skills early in a session — it's cheap (names and one-line descriptions only) and surfaces guidance not visible in any tool's name or schema. When a task matches a listed skill (e.g. debugging a build failure, tuning search_logs), call load_skill for that guide — it covers parameter tuning, caching behavior, and details beyond the summaries below.

Authorization: Tools available depend on the scopes and organization access granted to the configured API token. A 401 response means the token is invalid, expired, or revoked and requires reauthentication. A 403 response means the credentials were accepted but access was denied, commonly because the token lacks a required scope or organization access, or the user lacks permission.

Common pitfalls:

build_number is a sequential integer string (e.g. "42"), not a UUID. Build, job, artifact, and log tools all require this identifier — do not use the build's UUID id field.

Build failure investigation: start with get_build_failure_summary. It combines build state, blocking failed and canceled jobs, promised failures from running jobs, soft-failed jobs (listed after blocking failures and canceled jobs), bounded log tails, relevant annotations, and failed tests in one response; jobs that never ran (broken, waiting_failed, blocked_failed, unblocked_failed) fill the remaining max_jobs slots unless include_never_ran_jobs is false. Use the individual build, job, log, annotation, and test tools only when the summary identifies an area that needs deeper inspection.

Pipeline authoring: always check pipeline YAML with validate_pipeline before creating or updating a pipeline, or before committing changes to .buildkite/pipeline.yml. It validates against the official pipeline schema locally — the call itself never contacts the Buildkite API and works regardless of the configured token's scopes — and catches structural errors that would otherwise fail silently at upload time. A valid result does not guarantee runtime correctness (environment variable interpolation, plugin configuration, dynamically generated steps).

Build comparison: use compare_builds when asked what changed since a build worked, or to compare two builds. Without an explicit baseline it selects an earlier successful build on the same pipeline and branch. Report the selected baseline and unmatched steps; shared failing steps do not establish a shared cause or justify a retry. Timings cover final attempts, not total retry cost or build wall-clock duration.

Job state "broken" means the pipeline configuration decided, when the job was created, that it would not run: an `if` condition or `branches` filter did not match, `parallelism` was 0, or the step was marked `skip`. Broken is never caused by another job failing, never fails a build, and is normal in passing builds. Jobs stopped by a failed dependency are `waiting_failed`, `blocked_failed` or `unblocked_failed` instead; those appear only in builds that actually failed and are consequences of an upstream failure, not root causes. None of these four states ran, so they have no logs. `failed` = ran and exited non-zero; `skipped` = an external factor (e.g. a newer build superseded it). To explain a red build, investigate only `failed`, `timed_out`, `expired` jobs that are not `soft_failed`, as well as `running` jobs that have non-zero `promised_exit_status`.

Soft failures: a job with `soft_failed` true actually ran and exited unsuccessfully, but the step's `soft_fail` setting allowed that exit status, so the failure did not block the build. `soft_fail` may allow every non-zero exit or only listed `exit_status` values, so the same step can still fail … [truncated]

+- **`BootstrapLogger` now receives the bootstrap planning and progress lines.** They went only to the `-v` stderr log, so an embedder saw the GitHub size lookup and then nothing until the first checkpoint upload. A bootstrap that stalled while planning logged the size preflight and then nothing until its timeout. Every planning line now also goes to `BootstrapLogger`, with the logger's own attributes and the caller's context. Phase and checkpoint progress goes at Info: planning checkpoints, fetching the commit graph, planned remaining branches with their counts, push attempting, group pushed, branch finalized. Rejected pushes, unconfirmed creates and resume markers left on the target go at Warn. Lines logged once per branch (subsumed by trunk, already on target) go at Debug, so a repository with thousands of branches does not emit thousands of Info records per attempt. Error text from the target is sanitized. `-v` shows the same lines as before. ([#134](https://github.com/entireio/git-sync/pull/134))

- **Batched bootstrap of a repository with thousands of branches now makes progress.** It used to fetch the commit graph of every branch, one request per branch, before it pushed anything. On a branch-heavy repository that planning alone outlasted a 30-minute sync budget, so each attempt timed out with nothing on the target and started again (ENT-3617). The trunk is now planned and pushed first, so an attempt that times out still leaves it on the target. The remaining branches share one commit-graph fetch. Small branches are pushed in shared packs that create their refs directly, so a fetch and a push deliver many of them. A group whose pack is over budget splits in half. A branch too big to share a pack, or one with a resume marker, keeps its own checkpointed batch as before. `FetchCommitParents` now takes the wants as a list of hashes.

- **Replicate no longer gets stuck after an interrupted bootstrap.** Replicate routes to batched bootstrap only when every desired ref is missing on the target. A bootstrap cut short after the trunk landed left the next run on plain replicate, which sends every missing branch in one pack; a target with a request body limit refused it, and every retry sent the same pack again. When the target refuses replicate's pack for its size or a push deadline, replicate now creates the missing refs with batched bootstrap, planned in one commit-graph fetch against the refs the target already has, then pushes the remaining updates and deletes. Such a run reports relay reason `replicate-pack-rejected`.

- **SSH sources now negotiate protocol v2.** git-sync sent `GIT_PROTOCOL` as a prefix of the remote command, which hosts without a login shell reject (GitHub answers "Invalid command"), so `auto` fell back to v1 on every SSH sync and re-read the full ref advertisement on each RPC. It now sets `GIT_PROTOCOL` in the ssh environment and passes `-o SendEnv=GIT_PROTOCOL`, as git does. A server that does not accept the variable answers v0/v1 and `auto` falls back as before; `--protocol v2` against such a server fails with "source did not negotiate protocol v2". This includes servers that run a login shell but whose sshd does not list `GIT_PROTOCOL` in `AcceptEnv` (stock OpenSSH accepts only `LANG LC_*`): they used to reach v2 through the command prefix and now get v1, as they do with git itself, until `AcceptEnv GIT_PROTOCOL` is added.

content.text:
I fixed all seven review points in `6e8e5715`, with two caveats noted on #3 and #5, and pushed it. Tests and lint pass.

| # | Finding | What I did |
|---|---|---|
| 1 | Missing ctx | **Fixed.** Every log call now passes the caller's context, which meant adding a `ctx` parameter to `batchAfterPushError`, `keepMarker` and `checkpointsFromParents`. A new test (`TestPlanningLinesCarryCallerContext`) checks that each record reaches the logger with that context. |
| 2 | Group push failures at Info | **Fixed.** The group split and the "subdividing after target size rejection" line are now Warn, and so is the batched-mode retry. |
| 3 | Per-branch lines too noisy | **Fixed, partly.** "Subsumed by trunk", "already reachable on target" and "subsumed branch finalized" moved to Debug. The counts still go out at Info in "planned remaining branches", which now also logs when every branch is subsumed. I left "branch plan" and "branch finalized" at Info: grouped branches don't log them, so they only fire for branches pushed on their own. |
| 4 | Unsanitized error text | **Fixed.** `error` attributes and the kept-marker reason now pass through `sanitize.Line`. |
| 5 | Duplicate logging | **Fixed** for the size lookup. **Not fixed** for a logger and its `.With(...)` copy counting as two loggers: that can't happen through the public API, because `Logger` is only the internal `-v` logger. |
| 6 | Leftover-ref lines at Info | **Fixed.** "Keeping resume marker" and every "create unconfirmed" line are now Warn. |
| 7 | Simpler design | **Adopted.** One `slog.MultiHandler` combining the `-v` log and `BootstrapLogger` is built once in `Execute`. The three helper functions and the per-call opt-outs are gone. |

Fixing #3 changed one thing in `syncer.go`: the `-v` handler now accepts Debug, so `-v` still shows every line it showed before. Only the level labels differ, for lines that moved to Warn or Debug.

I also updated the CHANGELOG, the `BootstrapLogger` doc comment and the PR description, which still has no internal references.

These findings aren't on the trail or the PR as comments, so there was nothing to resolve there.

The Fable review found no wiring bugs, but my last commit promoted some lines to Warn too eagerly: a normal, successful large-repo bootstrap now emits Warn records. It ran tests and lint (both clean) and confirmed every record reaches each logger once, with the caller's context.

**Findings**
1. **Medium: a successful run emits Warns.** "push failed" (`bootstrap.go:827`) and "subdividing after target size rejection" (`:939`) also fire when git-sync stops a push itself because its own size estimate went over budget. That's the designed path for large repos, and the target rejected nothing. The reviewer reproduced it with the syncer test, which ends in success with two Warns. I checked the code: the Warn doesn't depend on whether the target actually rejected the push. A monitor on Warn would page on every big bootstrap.
   - Fix: use Info (with an accurate message) when git-sync stopped the push itself, and Warn only for a real rejection or timeout from the target, or when splitting can't help. The batched-mode retry (`:331`) is also a normal path and should be Info.
2. **Low: "create unconfirmed" Warns on targets that don't report per-ref status.** Usually the run settles it later at Info. The syncer wires up the confirmation, so only custom embedders hit this, but it's one Warn per branch.
   - Fix: log "deferring marker cleanup" at Info and keep Warn for `keepMarker`, the final verdict.
3. **Low: internal references in commit history.** This is the `e24cb70d` message I flagged earlier: INC-133, "the mirror worker", `target_ulid`. A squash merge also pre-fills its message from these commits.
4. **Low: docs overstate slightly.** "`-v` shows the same lines as before" is off by one new summary line, and "Warn for rejected pushes" is wrong because of finding 1.

**Rejected after checking:** lost or duplicated records, how the combined handler filters levels and passes context, preflight logging, sanitizing, test strength (the new tests fail on main), and the trailers.

I'd fix 1, 2 and 4 now. For 3, I'd reword `e24cb70d` with a force-push to the branch, or you squash with an edited message. Should I go ahead with 1, 2 and 4, and which way for 3?

A bootstrap that stalled while planning logged the size preflight and then nothing until its timeout. Every planning line now also goes to `BootstrapLogger`, with the logger's own attributes and the caller's context. Phase and checkpoint progress goes at Info: planning checkpoints, fetching the commit graph, planned remaining branches with their counts, push attempting, group pushed, branch finalized. A bootstrap that stalled while planning logged the size preflight and then nothing until its timeout. Every planning line now also goes to `BootstrapLogger`, with the logger's own attributes and the caller's context. Phase and checkpoint progress goes at Info: planning checkpoints, fetching the commit graph, planned remaining branches with their counts, push attempting, group pushed, branch finalized. A push the target refused or timed out, and resume markers left on the target, go at Warn; a push git-sync stops itself at its byte budget and then splits stays at Info, so a successful bootstrap logs no warnings. Lines logged once per branch (subsumed by trunk, already on target) go at Debug, so a repository with thousands of branches does not emit thousands of Info records per attempt. Error text from the target is sanitized. `-v` shows every line it showed before. ([#134](https://github.com/entireio/git-sync/pull/134))

- **Batched bootstrap of a repository with thousands of branches now makes progress.** It used to fetch the commit graph of every branch, one request per branch, before it pushed anything. On a branch-heavy repository that planning alone outlasted a 30-minute sync budget, so each attempt timed out with nothing on the target and started again (ENT-3617). The trunk is now planned and pushed first, so an attempt that times out still leaves it on the target. The remaining branches share one commit-graph fetch. Small branches are pushed in shared packs that create their refs directly, so a fetch and a push deliver many of them. A group whose pack is over budget splits in half. A branch too big to share a pack, or one with a resume marker, keeps its own checkpointed batch as before. `FetchCommitParents` now takes the wants as a list of hashes.

- **Replicate no longer gets stuck after an interrupted bootstrap.** Replicate routes to batched bootstrap only when every desired ref is missing on the target. A bootstrap cut short after the trunk landed left the next run on plain replicate, which sends every missing branch in one pack; a target with a request body limit refused it, and every retry sent the same pack again. When the target refuses replicate's pack for its size or a push deadline, replicate now creates the missing refs with batched bootstrap, planned in one commit-graph fetch against the refs the target already has, then pushes the remaining updates and deletes. Such a run reports relay reason `replicate-pack-rejected`.

- **SSH sources now negotiate protocol v2.** git-sync sent `GIT_PROTOCOL` as a prefix of the remote command, which hosts without a login shell reject (GitHub answers "Invalid command"), so `auto` fell back to v1 on every SSH sync and re-read the full ref advertisement on each RPC. It now sets `GIT_PROTOCOL` in the ssh environment and passes `-o SendEnv=GIT_PROTOCOL`, as git does. A server that does not accept the variable answers v0/v1 and `auto` falls back as before; `--protocol v2` against such a server fails with "source did not negotiate protocol v2". This includes servers that run a login shell but whose sshd does not list `GIT_PROTOCOL` in `AcceptEnv` (stock OpenSSH accepts only `LANG LC_*`): they used to reach v2 through the command prefix and now get v1, as they do with git itself, until `AcceptEnv GIT_PROTOCOL` is added.
